decks.title: Your story needs a buyer question.

slides.alt: Cover: Your story needs a buyer question.
Choose a question that matters. What is your buyer trying to decide before they can move forward?
Name a real decision. Pick a choice your team can describe accurately: what changed and why.
Show the trade-off. Explain the alternative you considered and what you gave up.
Give the reader a lesson. Turn that decision into a principle someone else can test.

decks.title: Make your positioning testable.

slides.alt: Cover: Make your positioning testable.
Name the team and task. Who uses the product, and what are they trying to get done?
Describe the real choice. A spreadsheet, an internal process or another product can all be alternatives.
Explain what changes. State one relevant difference. Support it with a demonstration or evidence.
Ask a buyer to repeat it. Could they explain the product and the relevant alternative in plain words?

decks.title: An AI claim needs a boundary.

slides.alt: Cover: An AI claim needs a boundary.
Show the actual workflow. Describe the input, the action and the output a user will see.
Say who verifies the result. Show the review step, escalation path or human decision where relevant.
Name the limitation. Be specific about conditions, exclusions and uncertainty.
Show evidence in context. Use a real example or measured result with its source, period and denominator.

decks.title: Explain the workflow around the model.

slides.alt: Cover: Explain the workflow around the model.
Begin with the trigger. What event or question starts the work?
Show the system's contribution. Describe what the product returns and where a person can inspect it.
Explain the next decision. What does the team do with the output?
Draw the path in four steps. Trigger, input, review, action. Label the human decision.

decks.title: One interview. Five useful angles.

slides.alt: Cover: One interview. Five useful angles.
What decision did you make? Ask for the context, the options and the people affected.
What did you rule out? The alternative and the reason can make the thinking concrete.
What can you show? Identify a safe example, a diagram or evidence the team can share.
Turn the answer into a series. Explain the choice, teach a method, compare options, clarify a limit, or answer an objection.

decks.title: Help buyers compare the options.

slides.alt: Cover: Help buyers compare the options.
Define the job. What must the team complete, and how will they know it is done?
Check the operating conditions. Consider inputs, security, implementation and the people involved.
Compare trade-offs. Show where each option fits and where it may not.
Make the decision visible. Give the buyer questions to take into their own evaluation.

decks.title: Two voices. One clear story.

slides.alt: Cover: Two voices. One clear story.
Share the judgment. Explain why a choice mattered and what the team learned.
Keep the facts accessible. Document the product workflow, updates, limitations and approved proof.
Answer the same buyer question. The founder's perspective and the company's explanation should reinforce each other.
Compare like with like. Use the same account, similar post age and the metrics actually available.

decks.title: Build a calendar around decisions.

slides.alt: Cover: Build a calendar around decisions.
Collect buyer questions. Use real sales, product and customer conversations where the team has permission.
Match each question to a voice. Choose the person or company source that can answer it accurately.
Add evidence and a format. Select a diagram, text, document or video for the explanation it enables.
Check the response. Compare similar posts over the same time window; record questions and limitations.

decks.title: What do LinkedIn reactions tell you?

slides.alt: Cover: What do LinkedIn reactions tell you?
Likes are one reaction type. The reaction total combines available reaction types. It does not include comments.
Replies are counted separately. A comment total is not unique people, qualified buyers or sales.
107.5 reactions. 36.5 comments. Medians: 276 observed reaction counts; 256 observed comment counts. 279 posts in the selected sample.
No reach. No conversion rate. We did not observe impressions, reach, clicks or sales. Reactions are not proof of buying intent.

decks.rights: Original graphic layouts with owner-selected Outspoken lockup and project-licensed fonts.

decks.title: Turn a response into a better question.

slides.alt: Cover: Turn a response into a better question.
Record what is visible. Keep reactions, comments and actual buyer conversations as separate measures.
Notice the question. Identify recurring confusion or objections without assigning intent to a reaction.
Bring it to the right expert. Ask the founder or product team for an accurate answer and source.
Make the next post clearer. Explain the answer, show relevant proof and retain the limits.
